nameStory: This vibrant wildflower earned its "scarlet" name from its brilliant red tubular flowers that practically glow in the forest. The "beebalm" part comes from its popularity with bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds who can't resist its nectar-rich blooms. Early colonists also called it "Oswego tea" after learning from the Oswego tribe how to brew its aromatic leaves into a minty tea.
description: Scarlet beebalm is a showy perennial wildflower that stands 2-4 feet tall with square stems typical of the mint family. Its most striking feature is the crown of brilliant red tubular flowers clustered at the top of each stem, creating a spiky, fireworks-like display. The plant has opposite pairs of serrated leaves that release a strong, pleasant minty fragrance when crushed. It spreads by underground stems to form colorful colonies that light up woodland edges and stream banks in midsummer.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant scarlet-red tubular flowers arranged in a dense, spiky cluster at the stem tip, each flower about 1-2 inches long with a distinctive curved shape that hummingbirds love

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite pairs of oval, serrated leaves that feel slightly fuzzy and release a strong, pleasant minty aroma when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Square stems that feel distinctly four-angled when rolled between your fingers, growing 2-4 feet tall in upright clumps

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Underneath the red flower cluster, look for reddish-tinged leafy bracts that add to the overall fiery appearance

habitat: Scarlet beebalm thrives in moist, rich soils along stream banks, woodland edges, and partially shaded meadows throughout New England. You'll often find it growing alongside ferns, wild ginger, and other moisture-loving plants in areas that stay consistently damp but not waterlogged. It prefers spots with morning sun and afternoon shade, making it common in the transition zones between forests and open areas.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge in late spring as fuzzy, square stems with small opposite leaves that already smell minty when crushed.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in mid to late summer (July-August) when the spectacular scarlet flower clusters appear, attracting clouds of bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade to brown seed heads, and leaves may turn yellowish before dying back, though the minty scent persists in dried foliage.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely to underground stems, leaving no above-ground trace until spring emergence.

funFact: Scarlet beebalm contains natural compounds that have antiseptic properties - Indigenous peoples used it to treat wounds and early colonists discovered that chewing the leaves could help prevent tooth decay and freshen breath, making it one of nature's original mouthwashes!
confusionNotes: The tubular red flowers and minty square stems make scarlet beebalm quite distinctive, but gardeners might confuse it with cardinal flower, which has brilliant red flowers but grows much taller with smooth round stems and no minty scent.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "bergamot," this plant is completely unrelated to the bergamot orange used to flavor Earl Grey tea - they just happen to share a similar citrusy-minty fragrance that reminded early botanists of each other.
compareHints: Scarlet beebalm is easily distinguished from its cousin wild bergamot by its brilliant red flowers (wild bergamot has pale pink or lavender blooms) and preference for moister soils. Unlike spotted horsemint with its yellow spotted flowers, scarlet beebalm's flowers are solid red and much more showy. The other beebalms in our region all lack that distinctive fire-engine red color that makes scarlet beebalm unmistakable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild bergamot differs from its flashier cousin scarlet beebalm by its pink-lavender flowers (versus bright red) and its preference for drier soils.
While wild bergamot and scarlet beebalm flaunt bright purple and red flowers respectively, spotted horsemint keeps a lower profile with cream-colored blooms.
Unlike scarlet beebalm's bright red flowers or wild bergamot's pale pink-purple blooms, lemon beebalm has distinctly tiered purple flower clusters.
Among New England's bergamots, purple bergamot is unique for its wetland habitat and reddish-purple flowers.
